sw_010:n1.prompt:
You are helping me audit this repository so it's ready for AI-agent-driven development. I'll be using {{vendor}} as my AI coding tool for this and later steps. If you need any details from me first — repo path/URL, primary language, existing build/test commands, or where docs live — ask before proceeding.

Please do the following:
1. Use {{vendor}}'s repo-map command (e.g. `{{vendor}} /map`) to generate and print a map of the codebase structure. Review it and summarize how the project is organized: main entry points, key modules/directories, and where a new contributor would start making a change.
2. Identify the build, lint, typecheck, and test commands currently defined in the repo (package.json scripts, Makefile, CI config, etc.). If a test command exists, run it via {{vendor}}'s run/test command (e.g. `{{vendor}} /test <test-command>` or `{{vendor}} /run <command>`) and capture the output, noting any failing or flaky tests.
3. Try to reproduce at least one known issue if one exists (check open issues or TODOs), or otherwise verify the current test suite passes cleanly — narrow down root cause of any failures you find.
4. Note any missing or unclear pieces: no test command, no lint/typecheck script, undocumented setup steps, or ambiguous entry points.

When done, report back with: (a) a short narrative map of the codebase, (b) the exact commands you found/ran for build, lint, typecheck, and test, with pass/fail status, (c) any reproduced issues and their likely root cause, and (d) a punch-list of gaps to fix before the repo is agent-ready (missing scripts, docs, flaky tests). Don't make code changes yet — this step is audit only.

sw_010:n2.prompt:
You are helping me make my codebase agent-ready by writing the project instructions file (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, matching whichever convention {{vendor}} expects) that sets coding standards and conventions for AI coding agents working in this repo. If you don't already have it, ask me for: my repo path or URL, the primary language(s)/framework(s), and any existing style guide, linting config, or contributing docs I already have.

Actions to take:
1. Inspect the repo structure, README, package/dependency manifests, and any existing lint/format/test configs to infer real conventions already in use (naming, folder layout, testing patterns).
2. Draft the instructions file covering: project overview and architecture summary, coding style and naming conventions, directory/file organization rules, how to run lint/typecheck/test commands, git commit/PR conventions, and any 'do not touch' areas or safety constraints.
3. Add a section describing available custom agent skills (or a placeholder list if none exist yet) so the agent knows what specialized tasks it can invoke.
4. Keep the file concise, scannable, and actionable — prefer bullet points and concrete commands over prose.
5. Save the file at the repo root using the filename convention {{vendor}} expects (e.g., AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md), and note if both are needed for compatibility.

Done looks like: a committed-ready draft file exists at the repo root, reflects the actual codebase conventions (not generic boilerplate), includes a skills section, and lists the exact lint/typecheck/test commands. Do not commit or push the file yourself — creating and staging the file locally is fine, but finalizing the commit remains a human step.

Report back with: the file path you created, a summary of the conventions and skills you documented, any assumptions you made where the repo was ambiguous, and a copy of the file contents for my review.

sw_010:n3.prompt:
You are helping me install an agent-skills stack ({{vendor}}) into my repo so any coding agent working here has a documented, reusable set of skills. 

First, ask me for: (1) my repo's local path or that we're already in it, (2) which coding agent harness(es) I use (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or multiple), (3) whether I want project-local install (files committed to the repo) or user-global (available across all my projects), and (4) whether I want the full {{vendor}} skills bundle or only specific skills from it — if specific, ask which ones.

Once I answer, do the following:
1. Check whether {{vendor}}'s CLI or marketplace mechanism is already available in this environment (via your configured credentials/tools); if not, note what's needed and proceed with what you can.
2. Search or list the available skills in {{vendor}}'s catalog and show me a short summary so I can confirm scope before installing (skip this if I already told you exactly which skills to install).
3. Run the documented one-line install command for {{vendor}}, using the scope and target harness(es) I specified, installing only the requested skills if I limited scope.
4. Verify the install succeeded by confirming the skill files/config are present in the expected location (project-local config directory or user-global directory) and, if {{vendor}} supports a lock/manifest file, confirm it was created or updated.
5. If installing for multiple harnesses, repeat per-harness install steps and confirm each one separately.

Done looks like: the skills stack is installed and active for the next session in each target harness, at the scope I chose, with only the skills I wanted present.

Report back: which harness(es) and scope you installed to, the exact command(s) run, confirmation of what got installed (list of skills), and any manual follow-up needed (e.g., restarting the agent session) for it to take effect.

sw_010:n4.prompt:
You are helping me wire one-line lint, typecheck, and test commands into my repository so an AI coding agent can reliably validate its own changes. If you don't already know it, ask me for my repo path/URL and the primary language(s)/framework(s) used (e.g., Node/TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust).

Actions to take:
1. Inspect the repo to detect existing tooling configs (e.g., package.json scripts, pyproject.toml, Makefile, tox.ini, Cargo.toml) and existing lint/typecheck/test setups (ESLint, Prettier, mypy, pytest, ruff, etc.).
2. If commands don't already exist, add or standardize simple, single-command entries for: lint (e.g., `npm run lint` or `make lint`), typecheck (e.g., `npm run typecheck` or `mypy .`), and test (e.g., `npm test` or `pytest`). Use whatever task runner already fits the repo's conventions (npm scripts, Makefile, justfile, tox, etc.) rather than introducing a new one unless none exists.
3. Ensure each command runs cleanly from a fresh clone with only standard dependency installation (document any setup step needed, like `npm install` or `pip install -e .`).
4. Update or create AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md (or the relevant conventions doc) to list these three exact one-line commands so an agent knows how to invoke them.
5. Run all three commands yourself locally to confirm they execute without errors (or fail only on genuine pre-existing lint/type/test issues, not on missing tooling).

Done looks like: three working one-line commands for lint, typecheck, and test exist, are documented in the agent conventions file, and you've verified each runs successfully (or reports real code issues, not setup errors).

Report back with: the exact three commands, where they're defined, what changes you made to config/docs files, and the output/status of running each command.

sw_010:n5.prompt:
You are helping me connect MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers for our stack's vendors using {{vendor}}, an MCP registry/infrastructure product, so our coding agent can call each vendor's tools directly.

First, ask me for: (1) the list of vendors/services our stack depends on that expose MCP servers (e.g., our database, CI, deploy, or issue-tracker vendors), (2) whether any of those already run a local MCP server I want bridged in versus one I want reached via a hosted remote URL, and (3) any tools that should be restricted or excluded per vendor for safety.

Once I provide that, do the following:
1. Use `{{vendor}} mcp search [term]` (or the registry's GET /servers search endpoint) to find the matching MCP server listing for each vendor in our stack.
2. For each candidate, inspect its listed tools, input schemas, transport type, and hosting attributes before connecting, and summarize these for me.
3. Connect each approved server using `{{vendor}} mcp add <url>` — using the hosted remote URL for vendors with managed servers, or bridging the local server as a managed remote connection if it's running locally.
4. Configure an allowlist so only the intended servers and specific tools are callable by our agent, per the restrictions I gave you.
5. Verify each connection is live and the agent can list the expected tools from it.

Done looks like every vendor in our stack has an MCP server connected and allowlisted, with no extraneous tools exposed.

Report back with: a table of vendor → connected server → tools allowlisted → transport/hosting type, plus any vendors where no suitable MCP server was found in the registry.

sw_010:n6.prompt:
You are helping me run a trial where {{vendor}}, our AI coding agent, ships one small fix end-to-end in this repo so we can validate our agent-ready setup. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the repo path or URL, (2) a specific small issue or bug to fix (or help me pick one from open issues), and (3) confirmation that {{vendor}} is configured with credentials in this environment.

Then: 1) Use {{vendor}} to implement the fix — either by creating a cloud agent via 'POST /v1/agents' targeting a PR, running the CLI non-interactively with 'agent -p "Your prompt here" --model gpt-5', or invoking it programmatically via 'Agent.create(...)' from TypeScript — whichever matches how {{vendor}} is installed here. Give it the issue description and repo context. 2) Have it create a branch, write the code changes across the relevant files, add/update tests, fix any lint errors, and write a clear commit message. 3) Run the repo's lint, typecheck, and test commands to confirm everything passes. 4) Have it open a pull request with a description of the change, and pull the diff so I can review it.

Done looks like: a branch and PR exist with the fix, tests and lint/typecheck all pass, and you have the diff and PR link ready for me to inspect.

Do not merge the PR, approve it, or apply the changes to the main branch yourself — a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied. Prepare the PR, diff, and check results, then stop for human sign-off. Report back the PR link, a summary of the diff, and the lint/typecheck/test results.

sw_010:n7.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for a team review meeting about guardrails and permissions for our AI coding agent (working in a repo we're making agent-ready with AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, lint/typecheck/test commands, and MCP server connections). The actual decision-making — engineers debating and agreeing on which repo actions and permissions are safe to expose to an autonomous agent — remains a human step and cannot be done by you.

Please prepare the materials so the team can have a productive discussion. Concretely:

1. Ask me for: repo name/URL, which CI/CD or hosting service we use (e.g. GitHub, GitLab), which MCP servers or integrations are already connected (e.g. filesystem, database, deployment), and any existing branch protection or CODEOWNERS rules.
2. Draft a one-page discussion doc listing: (a) proposed scope of agent actions (e.g. read code, open PRs, run tests, edit files, run migrations, deploy) with a recommended default (allow/deny/require-approval) for each; (b) which branches/environments the agent may touch (e.g. feature branches only, never main/production); (c) secrets and credential handling rules (agent should only use configured credentials, never read or output raw secrets); (d) required human checkpoints (e.g. PR review before merge, approval before deploy); (e) logging/audit requirements for agent actions.
3. Summarize any relevant constraints already visible in the repo (branch protection rules, required reviewers, existing CI gates) to ground the discussion in facts, not assumptions.
4. Compile open questions the team needs to resolve live (e.g. can the agent auto-merge, can it touch infra-as-code, rollback policy).

Output a single markdown document with these sections, ready to share before or during the meeting. Do not decide the policy yourself, approve any permission, or grant repo access — stop for human sign-off once the draft is ready, and report back that the document is prepared for team review.
